Modern.tagline: A modern store of considered things.
Modern.brandNameRationale: Halverson is a Scandinavian-rooted surname common across the American upper Midwest with a goods-and-trade register. Goods is the archaic plain category suffix used by 19th-century general stores. Stands in the lineage of heritage-modern DTC (Stutterheim, Fjällräven).
Modern.industrySummary: DTC ecommerce has been a category for a decade. The customer is tired of the playbook: linen ad copy, pastel boxes, founder origin stories. The next wave is curation-led marketplaces and design-forward retailers with editorial discipline.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Goop (goop.com) holds the celebrity-led curation peak. Need Supply Co. (now closed) was the design-led template. Verishop (verishop.com) sits in the contemporary tier. The Pop Up Grocer (popupgrocer.com) holds the discovery-shop position. We sit closest to Pop Up Grocer in posture, with sharper brand work.
Modern.positioningStatement: An online shop with limited shelves and editorial taste.

targetAudience.primary: 28 to 45. Reads two newsletters about shopping. Has bought from at least three DTC brands. Wants a curator to filter the noise. Will pay a premium for the editorial trust.

dos: Name the maker, the materials, and the reason it's on the shelf
Show why we picked it
Speak to the curator's reader, not the bargain hunter

Modern.logoDirection: A wordmark only. Halverson Goods in a tight modern grotesk, all caps, two words on one line. A small geometric mark, three thin horizontal lines stacked at irregular spacing to suggest a real shelf, used as the favicon and on the order tag.

colorPalette.name: Stamp Red
colorPalette.meaning: The single accent. The price flag.
colorPalette.usage: Hot products, sale signs, web headlines

typography.primary: GT America for the wordmark and headlines
typography.secondary: GT America Mono for product specs and prices
typography.rationale: One family. The mono carries the technical product data and price. The regular carries the brand.

customSections.title: What it doesn't do
customSections.body: No promotional codes. No 'final hours' urgency on the homepage. No affiliate-loaded influencer marketing. No flash sales.

customSections.title: Where it lives
customSections.body: A homepage that loads the editorial pick of the week. A monthly printed shelf guide mailed to subscribers. A pop-up shop in a different city twice a year. No referral program.

Modern.brandDescription: An online shop with limited shelves and editorial taste.
Modern.mission: To build an online shop with limited shelves and editorial taste.

Modern.tagline: A shop you'd actually send to a friend.
Modern.brandNameRationale: Cart is the retail action object; Crate is the warehouse object. Paired they ground the brand in honest retail logistics. Two-noun & paired naming follows considered DTC brand convention (Crate & Barrel, Stella & Chewy's).
Modern.manifesto: DTC brands have spent a decade trying to look like magazines. Long scroll pages, mood-board hero, founder story, materials breakdown, slow reveal. We made Shop Now because the customer is not here for the magazine. They are here to buy something. The site is short. The path is one click. The brand is the verb.
Modern.industrySummary: DTC e-commerce has converged on a soft-modern, story-led aesthetic. Conversion has dropped as the story has grown. There is a real opening for a brand that competes on speed-to-purchase and honesty about what it is.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Quince (onequince.com) holds the modern direct slot. Italic (italic.com) plays the membership-driven version. Brandless before its closure tried this lane. We sit further out — louder, less product-essay, more storefront.
Modern.positioningStatement: Shop Now is an online store that opens with the products, prices, and the buy button — and nothing else.
Modern.positioningRationale: We compete on conversion path length. The home page is a grid of products. Clicking a product opens a single page with price, photo, specs, and a single button.

targetAudience.primary: Returning online buyers 28–45 who do most of their shopping in five-minute windows on a phone.
behaviors: Re-buy the same items.
Skip the scroll on product pages.
Trust ratings over copy.
Abandon carts on three-step checkouts.
motivations: Want the price, the photo, the button.
Want a site that respects the five minutes they have.

dos: Lead with the price and the photo.
Skip founder stories on product pages.
Use the imperative — 'add to cart', 'reorder'.
Make the confirmation email one line.

messagingPillars.name: One-click buy
messagingPillars.description: Every product page has one CTA. The cart is one tap. The checkout is one screen. No upsells, no cross-sells, no shipping calculator drama.

messagingPillars.name: Re-order at the top
messagingPillars.description: Returning customers see their last three orders at the top of the home page. One tap re-buys.

messagingPillars.name: Plain product pages
messagingPillars.description: Each product page is a single image, a price, a paragraph of specs, and the button. The founder story is on the about page if you want it.

Modern.logoDirection: A wordmark — Cart & Crate Co set in a precise grotesque, all caps, with a small arrow appended to the W. Reads as a button at rest.

colorPalette.meaning: A single hot accent — only the CTAs.

typography.secondary: Same family for tables and code.
typography.rationale: One typeface across the whole shop. Hierarchy by weight only.

Luxury.brandNameRationale: Three words, two domestic anchors. Pantry and Hearth are older words for the two centers of a household: where the food is kept and where the fire is. The brand sits on the language of the home, told properly, before words like 'lifestyle' arrived.
Luxury.story: Pantry & Hearth began with a single editor who had spent years inside larger luxury retailers and wanted to keep a smaller shop. The shop took six months to fill. Each piece is chosen by the editor herself. The catalog is printed once a year.
Luxury.industrySummary: Top end home and lifestyle retail has been moving toward larger platforms and bigger drops. There's a parallel market for a smaller editorial shop that treats every object as a considered choice. The customer is paying for the curator, not the catalog.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: March (marchsf.com) holds the heritage independent home shop position. Toogood (t-o-o-g-o-o-d.com) sits in the design-led tier. Bergdorf Goodman Home (bergdorfgoodman.com) is the institutional reference. We sit closer to March in posture and intent.
Luxury.positioningStatement: A small editorial shop for objects meant to be kept.

targetAudience.primary: Wealthy. Often inherited. Owns at least one home they care about. Buys for the house slowly. Reads the catalog before buying. Knows the editor's taste.

dos: Name the maker and the material
Write product descriptions like museum cards
Send a paper card with every order
donts: Promote on Instagram with shoppable tags

Luxury.logoDirection: A classical serif wordmark with elegant ligatures. A small hand-drawn ampersand becomes the shop's hallmark, used on the catalog cover, the order card, and the wax seal of every paper letter.

colorPalette.name: Pantry Cream
colorPalette.meaning: Hand-laid paper, linen tea towel, the inside of a butter dish.

colorPalette.name: Hearth Black
colorPalette.meaning: Cast iron, the inside of the fireplace.

colorPalette.name: Heritage Brass
colorPalette.meaning: Aged metal. The hardware on the cabinets.

colorPalette.name: Olive
colorPalette.meaning: The garden outside the kitchen door.

typography.secondary: Söhne for the order portal and few digital surfaces
typography.rationale: A high contrast classical serif sets the heritage tone. A modern grotesk handles the order flow. Both restrained.

customSections.title: What it doesn't do
customSections.body: No flash sales. No promotional emails. No celebrity endorsements. No influencer affiliate programs. No same-day shipping.

Luxury.mission: To build a small editorial shop for objects meant to be kept.

Luxury.tagline: A small catalog, kept for years.
Luxury.brandNameRationale: Two surnames with uneven rhythms — Halsey reads as a Northeastern American name, Crowne reads as English. The pair sounds like a small firm that has been quietly trading for a long time. Avoids the standard 'House of [X]' luxury formula.
Luxury.story: Halsey & Crowne is a small online catalog of considered home, table, and travel goods. The catalog runs to 80 items. The founders pick every product personally. The catalog is updated twice a year, in spring and autumn.
Luxury.industrySummary: Premium e-commerce has split into the broad-aggregator slot (Net-a-Porter, MR PORTER) and the heavily branded vertical (Toteme, Khaite). There is a quieter market for the small considered catalog — twice a year, curator-led, no algorithm.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Magasin (magasin-marius.com) plays the small considered catalog. Toast (toa.st) holds the slow lifestyle slot. Mr Porter (mrporter.com) is the broad reference. We sit further down the catalog ladder — fewer items, longer kept.
Luxury.positioningStatement: Halsey & Crowne is a small twice-a-year catalog of considered objects for the home, the table, and the road.
Luxury.positioningRationale: We do not run promotions, refresh the site weekly, or follow trend cycles. The catalog is the product. The seasonal letter is the marketing.

targetAudience.primary: Buyers 35–60 who have stopped acquiring and are buying carefully.
behaviors: Re-read product pages weeks before buying.
Care about country of origin and maker.
Subscribe to printed catalogs.
Pass on most of what they consider.
motivations: Want to buy from a curator, not an algorithm.
Want things to keep for years.

dos: Write product copy in the founders' voice.

messagingPillars.description: The catalog is updated in spring and autumn. Between updates, the site is steady. New items are introduced in the seasonal letter, not by push notification.

messagingPillars.name: Kept, not bought
messagingPillars.description: Half the catalog has been on offer for more than three years. We do not retire items to make room for novelty.

Minimal.brandNameRationale: Single word. Checkout is the moment ecommerce is actually about. The brand sits on the action, not the catalog, not the brand world, not the founder story. Plain and honest about what the customer is doing.
Minimal.industrySummary: Most ecommerce sites have grown into content platforms, lookbooks, lifestyle hubs, and newsletters. There's an opening for one that strips it all back to the checkout itself.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: Most ecommerce brands compete on what they add. We compete on absence. The closest peers in spirit are some Japanese stationery shops and the early Muji digital experience.
Minimal.positioningStatement: An online shop with a checkout and not much else.

targetAudience.primary: Adults who don't want a relationship with the store. They want to find the product, buy it, and leave. They will resent any added screen.

dos: Show the product, the price, the buy button
Confirm the order in two lines
Print the return policy on the shipping label

Minimal.logoDirection: A wordmark only. CHECKOUT in a single weight grotesk, wide kerned, all caps. No icon. The favicon is the wordmark abbreviated to a small chevron. The order confirmation, the shipping label, and the return form all use the same wordmark.

typography.rationale: One face. The product page is the wordmark, the photo, the price, the buy button. Nothing else.

customSections.title: Not this

Minimal.brandDescription: An online shop with a checkout and not much else.

Minimal.tagline: A small online store of plain things.
Minimal.brandNameRationale: Carton is the real packaging word — single trade noun, archaic in casual speech, immediately readable in retail context. Single-word naming follows the minimal DTC school (Italic, Quince).

We made Carton because the customer already decided. The site shows the product. The button is at the top. The end.
Minimal.industrySummary: DTC has over-engineered the product page. There is room for a brand that strips the page to a photograph, a price, and a button — and trusts the customer to know what they came for.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: Italic (italic.com) plays the minimal-direct slot at scale. Quince (onequince.com) holds the basics-direct middle. Brandless attempted this position. We sit further out — fewer products, less language, the button at the top.

Corporate.brandNameRationale: Apex suggests the highest point of performance. Commerce names the category. Partners closes it as a B2B service relationship. The whole name reads like a real, established ecommerce services firm, already on the procurement panel at Fortune 500 retailers.
Corporate.industrySummary: Enterprise ecommerce infrastructure is a multi-billion-dollar B2B category. Retailers, brands, and marketplaces need partners for platform implementation, integration, fulfillment, and analytics. The category is dominated by giant systems integrators with high overhead. There's a clear opening for a structured mid-size firm.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: Salesforce Commerce Cloud (salesforce.com/products/commerce-cloud) is the platform giant. BORN Group (borngroup.com) holds the systems integrator peer. Accenture Interactive (accenture.com/song) sits in the consulting-led tier. Shopify Plus (shopify.com/plus) handles the mid-market platform side. We sit smaller than these giants, more design-led than the integrators.
Corporate.positioningStatement: Ecommerce infrastructure and implementation for mid-market enterprise retailers.
Corporate.positioningRationale: Mid-market retailers are too small for Accenture and too sophisticated for boutique agencies. We sit in the middle, with the operating discipline they need and the responsiveness the integrators can't deliver.

targetAudience.primary: VPs of Ecommerce, Chief Digital Officers, and CTOs at retailers, brands, and marketplaces of $50M to $5B in annual revenue. They sign multi-year contracts.
motivations: Integration across the full ecommerce stack
Reporting that connects platform investment to revenue

dos: Lead with platform certifications and case study revenue impact

messagingPillars.name: Reporting that connects to revenue
messagingPillars.description: Platform investment measured against gross merchandise value, conversion, and customer lifetime value.

typography.rationale: Inter scales clean across digital. The serif handles formal quarterly business reviews and printed implementation playbooks.

Corporate.tagline: Multi-brand online retail and fulfillment, mid-market.
Corporate.brandNameRationale: Marston is a surname with a steady, slightly establishment register. Retail Group signals the category and the holding structure. The pair reads as a serious multi-brand operator with a regional warehouse footprint.
Corporate.manifesto: Marston Retail Group is a multi-brand online retailer with shared fulfillment, customer service, and merchandising operations. Brands keep their identities; we keep them stocked, shipped, and supported. The buyer is a brand founder who needs operational scale without losing the brand they built.
Corporate.industrySummary: Mid-market DTC brands face rising acquisition costs and stretched fulfillment economics. The opening is for an operator that consolidates the back office across multiple brands and provides shared fulfillment, customer service, and merchandising, while the brands retain their public identities.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: Pattern (pattern.com) plays in the e-commerce operator slot. Win Brands Group (winbrandsgroup.com) is the peer. Berlin Brands Group (berlinbrandsgroup.com) holds the European reference. We sit in the regional multi-brand operator middle.
Corporate.positioningStatement: Marston Retail Group is a regional multi-brand online retailer operating fulfillment, customer service, and merchandising across a portfolio of consumer brands.
Corporate.positioningRationale: We compete on fulfillment economics, customer-service depth, and merchandising data — across multiple brands under one operations team.

Creative.tagline: A shop with a sense of humor about being a shop.
Creative.brandNameRationale: Storefront is the trade word for the public-facing surface of a retail business. The definite article + Co suffix follows the considered-creative trade naming school.
Creative.manifesto: Most ecommerce brands lead with abundance: infinite inventory, infinite scrolls, infinite emails. We lead with scarcity. The drop ends. The shelf empties. The customer is part of the moment, not the campaign. Sold Out is the brand for people who want to be there when it happens.
Creative.industrySummary: Ecommerce branding has been clean, polished, and slightly cold. There's room for a brand that treats every drop as an event, brings personality back to the product page, and makes the buying itself feel like a story.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Supreme (supremenewyork.com) holds the drop-culture peak. Aimé Leon Dore (aimeleondore.com) has the cultural-product hybrid position. Off-White (off---white.com) sits in the fashion-meets-drops tier. We are smaller, more playful, and category-agnostic.
Creative.positioningStatement: An ecommerce brand that treats every product as a small event.

targetAudience.primary: 20s and 30s. Already buys from at least one drop brand. Sets push notifications. Tells friends about the brand on close-friends stories. Buys the merch.

dos: Make jokes about scarcity
Show the count down
Tell the customer the truth about what's left
donts: Apologize for things being sold out

Creative.logoDirection: A wordmark in a punchy display serif with the O of SOLD set as a small filled dot, like a sold-out indicator. Standalone filled-dot icon for app icons, social profiles, and the back of every shipped box.

Creative.tagline: An online store built around the second time.
Creative.brandNameRationale: Reorder is the proper retail trade word for placing a follow-on purchase. & Co follows the small-shop trade-name convention. The brand stakes a position on customer retention rather than acquisition.
Creative.manifesto: DTC marketing has been pretending shopping is anything other than what it is. Wellness, lifestyle, community, identity. We made Add To Cart because shopping is fun in a small specific way — finding a thing, deciding to buy it, watching it arrive. We named the brand after the click and kept the rest of the experience honest about what it is.
Creative.industrySummary: DTC marketing has drifted into identity work. Customers are noticing. There is a real opening for a brand that calls the activity what it is and trades on the small specific pleasures of shopping itself.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Glossier (glossier.com) defined community-led DTC. Parade (yourparade.com) holds the playful-identity slot. Brandless tried the opposite extreme. We sit further out — meta about the act of shopping itself.
Creative.positioningStatement: Add To Cart is a small online shop that is honest about being a shop — the click, the box, the unboxing.
Creative.positioningRationale: The brand names the act. The packaging celebrates the act. The marketing is the unboxing video.

targetAudience.primary: Adults 25–40 who shop online for fun and don't pretend otherwise.
behaviors: Save tabs of things they want.
Watch unboxing videos for entertainment.
Re-buy favorites.
Order things they probably did not need.
motivations: Want a shop that gets the joke.
Want the small pleasure of the click.

dos: Celebrate the click.
Talk about the box.

messagingPillars.name: The box matters
messagingPillars.description: Every order ships in a printed box that names what the customer just did. The unboxing is part of the product.

messagingPillars.name: The wishlist is the marketing
messagingPillars.description: Customers build wishlists. Wishlists are public if they want them to be. The wishlist is the brand on a Friday night.

messagingPillars.name: Confirmation as celebration
messagingPillars.description: The confirmation email reads like a friend congratulating the customer. The shipping email tracks the box like an event.

Creative.logoDirection: A wordmark — Reorder & Co set in a wide modern grotesque, all caps, with a small cart icon at the end. Used at huge scale on the box.

colorPalette.name: Hot Pink
colorPalette.usage: Wordmark, the cart icon, the box.

typography.primary: A wide modern grotesque for the wordmark and the box.
typography.secondary: A neutral sans for working type.
typography.rationale: The wordmark is loud. The body is calm. Both are friendly.

Creative.brandDescription: Add To Cart is a small online shop that is honest about being a shop — the click, the box, the unboxing.
Creative.mission: The brand names the act. The packaging celebrates the act. The marketing is the unboxing video.
Creative.vision: We named the brand after the click and kept the rest of the experience honest about what it is.
coreValues: Warm — we are friendly, not formal.
A little cheeky — a core principle the brand operates by.
Modern — we build for the customer reading this on a phone.
Specific — generalities are how people avoid commitment.
